question: In Valencia, there are 10 286 illegal tourist apartments. This is having a devastating effect on the city’s residents and neighbourhoods. Unbridled tourism strips neighbourhoods of traditional businesses, forces out their inhabitants, puts a strain on community relations, makes it difficult to access the right to housing, encourages property speculation and pushes up rents.

Our cities and neighbourhoods find themselves pitted against the interests of EU-wide multinationals which, allied with local rent-seeking elites, are causing serious social damage to workers, families and young people. The unbridled tourism that is hollowing out Valencia’s neighbourhoods is an unsustainable social, economic and ecological model. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission planning to create a tourism strategy based on solidarity and territorial, ecological and economic respect?
Why does the Commission not establish a European tourist tax that could be collected and managed at the municipal level?
How will the Commission ensure that Spain’s autonomous communities comply with the regulation on short-term rental services in order to expose illegal properties?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.8.2024) Sustainable and resilient tourism is at the core of the Transition pathway for tourism1 and the European Agenda for Tourism 20302. One of the key actions promoted in the transition pathway is the development of national and regional strategies that take account of the economic, environmental and social sustainability of tourism.

The Regulation on short-term accommodation rental services (STR)3 will enable local authorities to enforce effective and proportionate rules, including with respect to illegal listings. The Commission is not planning to establish a harmonised European tourist tax as Member States and regions are free to apply measures that are most suitable for their circumstances.

However, two Commission proposals are of relevance: one requires reporting platforms operators to report information on certain sellers that carry out activities involving the rental of immovable property4; another one makes platforms responsible for charging the Value Added Tax (VAT) where the underlying supplier does not5.

Both allow for the correct assessment of taxes and equalisation of treatment between the traditional and platform sectors. The STR Regulation requires Member States to designate an authority to monitor the implementation of its obligations. It is the responsibility of the Spanish authorities to ensure that the autonomous communities comply with that regulation.

To help competent authorities identify illegal listings, online platforms are required to design their websites in a userfriendly way so as to facilitate hosts to display and check registration numbers and share their data on a monthly basis, with the competent authorities. The Commission will monitor the implementation of the regulation by Member States.
